clinicalPearls: MVP is a clinically variable syndrome arising from diverse pathologic mechanisms affecting the mitral valve apparatus, commonly excessive or redundant leaflet tissue associated with myxomatous degeneration and increased glycosaminoglycan concentrations (p.2057).

It is the most common abnormality leading to primary mitral regurgitation and to mitral valve repair surgery, and in North America is now the most common cause of isolated severe MR requiring surgery (p.2057-2058).

MVP is more common in women than men and typically presents between ages 15 and 30 with a generally benign course; in older patients (>50 years, often men) MR tends to be more severe because of chordal rupture (p.2058).

The posterior leaflet is usually more affected than the anterior, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae tendineae frequently cause or contribute to regurgitation (p.2058).

The hallmark auscultatory finding is a mid- or late nonejection systolic click occurring 0.14 s or more after S1, often followed by a high-pitched mid-late systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the apex, sometimes described as whooping or honking (p.2058).

Dynamic auscultation aids diagnosis: standing, the strain phase of Valsalva, and any maneuver decreasing LV volume make the click and murmur occur earlier, whereas squatting and isometric exercise (increasing LV volume) delay the click-murmur complex and may make it disappear (p.2058).

Murmur radiation depends on the leaflet involved: posterior leaflet prolapse directs the jet anteriorly with radiation toward the base, while anterior leaflet involvement directs the jet posteriorly with radiation to the axilla and back (p.2058).

A useful echocardiographic definition is systolic displacement of the belly of the mitral leaflets by at least 2 mm into the left atrium above the plane of the mitral annulus in the parasternal long-axis view (p.2058).
Chest pain in MVP is often substernal, prolonged, and unrelated to exertion, and only rarely resembles angina pectoris (p.2058).
Most patients are asymptomatic and remain so for life; the disease may progress slowly over years to decades or worsen abruptly from chordal rupture or endocarditis (p.2058).
MVP can occur as a rare sequel to acute rheumatic fever, in ischemic heart disease, in various cardiomyopathies, and in about 20% of patients with ostium secundum atrial septal defect (p.2058).
harrison.pathophysiology: MVP results from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve apparatus with excessive or redundant leaflet tissue and markedly increased glycosaminoglycan content. In many cases the cause is unknown, but some forms are genetically determined; reduced type III collagen production has been implicated, and electron microscopy shows fragmentation of collagen fibrils. Genome-wide association work has identified multiple genetic loci (candidate genes include LMCD1, SPTBN1, LTBP2, TGFB2, NMB, and ALPK3), and associations with LMNA, FLNC, and FLNA that are often expressed as cardiomyopathies. The posterior leaflet is typically more affected, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae contribute to regurgitation. Prolapse may impose excessive stress on the papillary muscles, producing localized ischemia, infarction, and replacement fibrosis that can serve as a nidus for ventricular arrhythmias (visible as late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI even without coronary disease). Chordal rupture along with progressive annular dilation and calcification worsen regurgitation, placing further stress on the diseased apparatus in a self-perpetuating cycle (p.2057-2058).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation
Rheumatic mitral valve disease (chordae thickened but not fused in MVP, unlike rheumatic disease)
Angina pectoris (when atypical chest pain is present)
additionalInvestigations: ECG (often normal; may show biphasic or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF and supraventricular or ventricular premature beats)
Transthoracic echocardiography to identify abnormal leaflet position and prolapse and define the >=2 mm displacement criterion
Color flow and continuous-wave Doppler to assess associated MR and estimate severity
Three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MRI for more precise LV volumes and detection of papillary muscle fibrosis/late gadolinium enhancement
Transesophageal echocardiography when detailed anatomy is needed and for intraoperative or transcatheter procedural guidance
Exercise testing (often with rest and immediate poststress TTE) to assess functional capacity, LV/RV function, dynamic MR, and pulmonary pressures
redFlags: Severe MR with depressed LV systolic function (highest risk for sudden death)
Flail leaflet, which carries an excess risk of sudden death and usually accompanies severe MR
High-grade ventricular ectopy with inferior-apical T-wave abnormalities, high-density premature ventricular complexes at rest, mitral annular disjunction, and papillary muscle fibrosis on cardiac MRI
Transient ischemic attacks from emboli due to endothelial disruption on the valve
Features suggesting infective endocarditis in patients with MR and/or leaflet thickening
harrison.prognosis: The clinical course is most often benign, and the majority of patients remain asymptomatic for their entire lives. In many the condition progresses gradually over years to decades, while in others it worsens rapidly from chordal rupture or endocarditis. Sudden death is a very rare complication, occurring most often with severe MR and depressed LV systolic function but possible even with normal LV size and function; a small high-risk subset has high-grade ventricular ectopy with characteristic imaging features, and patients with a flail leaflet carry an excess sudden-death risk (p.2058).
pitfalls: Relying on a static exam can miss MVP; the click and murmur are dynamic and shift with maneuvers that alter LV volume (Valsalva/standing exaggerate, squatting/isometrics diminish them).
Presentations vary: some patients have a mid-systolic click without a murmur, others a murmur without a click, and still others both at different times.
The eccentric MR jet typical of MVP makes effective regurgitant orifice area and regurgitant volume difficult to assess with standard techniques.
Atypical, prolonged, non-exertional chest pain may be misattributed to coronary disease and is often difficult to evaluate.
Sudden death and significant arrhythmias can occur even in patients with normal LV size and function, so apparently low-risk patients are not entirely without risk.
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is anchored on the associated mitral regurgitation, ranging from a benign isolated systolic click with mild posterior-leaflet prolapse to severe MR from chordal rupture and leaflet flail. Echocardiographic prolapse is defined as >=2 mm systolic displacement of the leaflet belly into the left atrium above the annular plane (parasternal long-axis), with Doppler used to grade MR severity (p.2058).
management: Reassurance and periodic observation for the majority with benign asymptomatic prolapse and no significant regurgitation
Beta-blockers for symptomatic palpitations, chest pain and autonomic symptoms
Mitral valve repair for severe primary MR complicating prolapse, particularly after chordal rupture, following the same timing principles as degenerative MR

Surveillance for and management of ventricular arrhythmias in arrhythmic mitral valve prolapse with mitral annular disjunction and papillary muscle fibrosis, using antiarrhythmic drugs or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in those at high risk of sudden death
Serial echocardiography to monitor leaflet morphology, progression of regurgitation and left-ventricular size and function, at intervals guided by severity
Attention to dental and skin hygiene for endocarditis prevention, with antibiotic prophylaxis reserved for the highest-risk subgroups per current guidance
Genetic evaluation and family screening where a heritable syndromic or familial form is suspected
